claim: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) affects over eight million individuals worldwide with an estimated 0.5 million new diagnoses each year.
source: In type 1 diabetes (T1D), insulin-producing β-cells are killed by islet-infiltrating immune cells in a process called 'insulitis'. T1D results in a critical requirement for exogenous insulin and affects over eight million individuals world-wide with an estimated 0.5 million new diagnoses each year (Gregory et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gregory et al., 2022

claim: Teplizumab (a human anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody) was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration as the first immunotherapy for delaying T1D onset.
source: Recently, the first immunotherapy for delaying T1D onset, teplizumab (a human anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody) was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (Hirsch, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirsch, 2023

claim: Teplizumab and other immunotherapies help only a small fraction of patients and are significantly less effective after patients progress to overt T1D.
source: However, this treatment and other immunotherapies help only a small fraction of patients and are significantly less effective after patients progress to overt T1D (Herold et al., 2013; Perdigoto et al., 2019; Herold et al., 2019; Pescovitz et al., 2009; Orban et al., 2011; Orban et al., 2014; Bluestone et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies

claim: The JDRF Network for Pancreatic Organ Donors with Diabetes (nPOD) provides human pancreatic tissues from cadaveric donors.
source: Fortunately, the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation (JDRF) Network for Pancreatic Organ Donors with Diabetes (nPOD) provides human pancreatic tissues from cadaveric donors for this study and many others (Campbell-Thompson et al., 2012; Pugliese et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campbell-Thompson et al., 2012 and Pugliese et al., 2014

claim: The abundance of multiple types of immune cells outside islets are increased in T1D patients compared to non-T1D controls.
source: First, the abundance of multiple types of immune cells outside islets are increased in T1D patients compared to non-T1D controls (Rodriguez-Calvo et al., 2014; Campbell-Thompson et al., 2015; Bender et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rodriguez-Calvo et al., 2014; Campbell-Thompson et al., 2015; Bender et al., 2020

claim: HLA-DR expression is increased on ductal cells in T1D tissue donors.
source: Second, HLA-DR expression is increased on ductal cells in T1D tissue donors, hinting at a functional link with CD4+T cells (Fasolino et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fasolino et al., 2022

claim: Peri-insulitis, the accumulation of immune cells outside islets, is observed in tissues from patients with T1D.
source: Third, peri-insulitis, the accumulation of immune cells outside islets, is observed in tissues from patients with T1D Korpos et al., 2013, indicating that not all T cells enter the pancreas directly via islet microvasculature (Savinov et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korpos et al., 2013 and Savinov et al., 2003

claim: In human T1D, islets in different regions of the pancreas are infiltrated at strikingly different rates.
source: Fourth, in human T1D, but less so in most animal models, islets in different regions of the pancreas are infiltrated at strikingly different rates for reasons that are unknown (In't Veld, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to In't Veld, 2014

claim: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) are observed outside islets in T1D patients.
source: Finally, tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) — dense aggregates of lymphoid cells indicative of local immune activation — are observed outside islets in T1D patients (Korpos et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Korpos et al., 2021

claim: The study used CO-Detection by indexing (CODEX) with an antibody panel targeting 54 antigens.
source: Here, we investigated the islet and extra-islet pancreas together. We used CO-Detection by indexing (CODEX) with an antibody panel targeting 54 antigens to samples from a cohort of T1D patients with insulitis as well as non-T1D individuals with and without islet-specific autoantibodies (AA- and AA+ respectively) obtained through the JDRF nPOD program.
evidence: Direct statement of methodology used in the study

claim: The study analyzed approximately 2000 islets.
source: We analyzed approximately 2000 islets and broad swaths of the extra-islet tissue to evaluate local and distal spatial architecture.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of islets analyzed

claim: At the time of the study, only 17 of close to 200 T1D cases in nPOD had documented insulitis.
source: Insulitis is present in most newly diagnosed T1D cases but in only a small fraction of total T1D cases, including those available from nPOD (In't Veld, 2011; Atkinson and Mirmira, 2023). Although nPOD had close to 200 T1D cases, at the time of our study, only 17 had documented insulitis.
evidence: Direct statement about the cohort selection process, with supporting citations

claim: The final cohort included two AA+ cases, eight T1D cases, and three non-T1D controls.
source: The final cohort included two AA+ cases, eight T1D cases, and three non-T1D controls.
evidence: Direct statement of cohort composition

claim: The T1D cases varied in the time between diagnosis and death from 0 years (diagnosed at death) to 6 years.
source: The T1D cases varied in the time between diagnosis and death from 0 years (diagnosed at death) to 6 years (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Large regions averaging 55 mm2 were imaged with CODEX.
source: Large regions averaging 55 mm2 were imaged with CODEX as previously described (Schürch et al., 2020; Phillips et al., 2021a; Hickey et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct statement of imaging area with supporting citations

claim: The dataset consisted of 7.0x10^6 cells across all donors.
source: In total, our dataset consisted of 7.0x106 cells across all donors (ranging from 3.0x105 to 9.8x105 cells per donor).
evidence: Direct statement of total cell count in the dataset

claim: Twenty-one cell types were identified with Leiden clustering and manual merging.
source: Twenty-one cell types were identified with Leiden clustering and manual merging and visualized using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP; Figure 1B; Table 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1B and Table 2

claim: Samples from patients who had been diagnosed with T1D for 0–2 years had significantly reduced β-cell frequencies compared to non-T1D controls.
source: Similarly, we found that samples from patients who had been diagnosed with T1D for 0–2 years had significantly reduced β-cell frequencies compared to non-T1D controls.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding

claim: Samples from subjects with disease durations of 5–6 years had minimal remaining β-cell mass.
source: Furthermore, samples from subjects with disease durations of 5–6 years had minimal remaining β-cell mass (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1D

claim: Donors were clearly separated into two groups by the first two principal components based on the abundances of non-endocrine cell types located in islets.
source: We performed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the donors using the frequencies of non-endocrine cell types located in islets. Donors were clearly separated into two groups by the first two principal components; one group included all T1D cases and one AA+ case and the second included all non-T1D cases and the other AA+ case (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct statement of PCA results with reference to Figure 1E

claim: Both the islet and extra-islet spaces of T1D and non-T1D cases were distinct.
source: Therefore, both the islet and extra-islet spaces of T1D and non-T1D cases were distinct.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from PCA analysis of both compartments

claim: In human T1D, β-cell destruction does not occur simultaneously across all islets.
source: In human T1D, β-cell destruction does not occur simultaneously across all islets and even neighboring islets can be at different stages of destruction (Damond et al., 2019; In't Veld, 2014; In't Veld, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Damond et al., 2019; In't Veld, 2014; In't Veld, 2011

claim: Pseudotime analysis using PAGA identified a continuum from islets abundant in insulin-expressing β-cells to islets depleted in β-cells.
source: In the PAGA map, a continuum is apparent from islets abundant in insulin-expressing β-cells on the left of the map to islets depleted in β-cells on the right (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, top row).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to multiple figures showing the continuum

claim: Islets were labeled into three groups: Normal, Inflamed, and Insulin-Depleted based on PAGA-internal Leiden clustering.
source: PAGA uses Leiden clustering internally, enabling the following regions of the pseudotime map to be labeled objectively: (1) Islets with low pseudotime values on the left of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 0 and 5 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were labeled 'Normal' even if they originated from T1D donors. (2) Islets in the middle of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 6, 2, and 8 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were elevated in HLA-ABC (MHC Class I) expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, rows 2–4) and were labeled 'Inflamed'. (3) Islets with late pseudotime values on the right of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 1, 3, 7, and 4 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were devoid of β-cells and were labeled 'Insulin-Depleted' (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, top row).
evidence: Direct statement of classification method with references to figures

claim: Inflamed islets were elevated in HLA-ABC (MHC Class I) expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs.
source: Islets in the middle of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 6, 2, and 8 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were elevated in HLA-ABC (MHC Class I) expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, rows 2–4) and were labeled 'Inflamed'.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures showing elevated markers

claim: Immune cells were targeting islets specifically, as demonstrated by increased fractions of B cells, CD4+T cells, CD8+T cells, macrophage/DCs, neutrophils, and plasma cells in islets relative to outside the islets.
source: We quantified the fraction of each cell type in swaths at varying distances from the islet edge. We found that for B cells, CD4+T cells, CD8+T cells, macrophage/DCs, neutrophils, and plasma cells, the fraction of the given cell type in the islet relative to outside the islets increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that the inflammation in islets was distinct from the inflammation in the extra-islet tissue. Thus, immune cells were targeting islets specifically.
evidence: Direct statement based on spatial analysis with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The results illustrate a single, non-branching progression from Normal Islets to Insulin-Depleted Islets via Inflamed Islets.
source: Together, these results illustrate a single, non-branching progression from Normal Islets to Insulin-Depleted Islets via Inflamed Islets, consistent with previous pseudotime analyses (Damond et al., 2019).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from pseudotime analysis, supported by citation to Damond et al., 2019

claim: IDO expression on islet vasculature was observed in islets.
source: We observed islets in which CD31+ vasculature stained positive for indoleamine 2, 3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data

claim: In islets, IDO did not co-stain with CD45+ immune cells adjacent to vasculature.
source: In islets, IDO did not co-stain with CD45+ immune cells adjacent to vasculature (Figure 2G).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2G

claim: IDO expression was not observed in endocrine or other cell types in islets or in vasculature or any cell type outside islets.
source: We did not observe IDO expression in endocrine or other cell types in islets or in vasculature or any cell type outside islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: All but two IDO+ islets were in the Inflamed group.
source: We manually quantified vascular expression of IDO in islets throughout pseudotime and found that all but two IDO+ islets were in the Inflamed group (Figure 2H).
evidence: Direct statement of quantification results shown in Figure 2H

claim: IDO expression by islet vasculature was tightly associated with insulitis.
source: Therefore, IDO expression by islet vasculature was tightly associated with insulitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that IDO+ islets were predominantly in the Inflamed group

claim: CD8+T cells were significantly more abundant in islets with IDO+ vasculature than islets without IDO+ vasculature.
source: We compared the frequency of CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs in islets from the Inflamed group with and without IDO+ vasculature and found that CD8+T cells were significantly more abundant in islets with IDO+ vasculature than islets without IDO+ vasculature (Figure 2I).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison shown in Figure 2I

claim: The expression of HLA-ABC was higher in β-cells in IDO+ islets than in β-cells in IDO– islets.
source: In addition, the expression of HLA-ABC, another interferon-stimulated gene, was higher in β-cells in IDO+ islets than in β-cells in IDO– islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Direct statement of comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: The abundance of macrophage/DCs was not significantly associated with IDO+ vasculature.
source: However, the abundance of γδ-T cells and CD4+T cells was less strongly associated with IDO+ vasculature and the abundance of macrophage/DCs was not significantly associated with IDO+ vasculature (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: IDO expression by islet vasculature is positively associated with T cell infiltration and may be an immunoregulatory checkpoint in T1D.
source: In summary, IDO expression by islet vasculature is positively associated with T cell infiltration and may be an immunoregulatory checkpoint in T1D.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the association between IDO+ vasculature and CD8+T cell abundance

claim: A neural network was trained on manually labeled images of single T cells to quantify the expression of T cell markers on islet CD8+T cells.
source: To obtain extremely high-quality marker quantification, we trained a neural network on manually labeled images of single T cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Using our neural network, we quantified the expression of T cell markers on islet CD8+T cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement of methodology with references to figures

claim: PD-1, TOX, CD45RO, CD69, and CD44, markers of antigen experience, were the markers most frequently expressed by islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells.
source: PD-1, TOX, CD45RO, CD69, and CD44, markers of antigen experience, were the markers most frequently expressed by islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures showing marker expression

claim: CD8+T cells expressing CD45RA were detectable in islets.
source: CD8+T cells expressing CD45RA (which are either naive or terminally differentiated effector memory cells [TEMRA]) were detectable in islets, as previously reported (Damond et al., 2019; Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct observation with reference to Figure 3B and citation to Damond et al., 2019

claim: A rare population of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells co-expressing LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS was observed.
source: In addition, we observed a rare population of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells co-expressing LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS (P bottom clade).
evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis

claim: A rare population of CD57+/CD8+T cells was present but these cells rarely co-expressed LAG-3, Granzyme-B, or ICOS.
source: Lastly, a rare population of CD57+/CD8+T cells was present but these cells rarely co-expressed LAG-3, Granzyme-B, or ICOS (Figure 3B top clade).
evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The activation profiles of islet-infiltrating T cells are heterogeneous.
source: Therefore, the activation profiles of islet-infiltrating T cells are heterogeneous.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation of multiple distinct T cell populations

claim: Four inflamed sub-clusters (I–IV) were identified based on the frequencies of CD8+T cells expressing each functional marker.
source: To interrogate this, we performed UMAP only on Inflamed islets, using the frequencies of CD8+T cells expressing each functional marker. We identified four inflamed sub-clusters, I–IV, (Figure 3C top).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3C

claim: Inflamed-I contained only CD8+T cells that did not express any of the functional markers analyzed.
source: Inflamed-I contained only CD8+T cells that did not express any of the functional markers analyzed (Figure 3C bottom, top row).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3C

claim: Inflamed-II was characterized by a high frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells.
source: Inflamed-II was characterized by a high frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells (Figure 3C bottom, second row from top and Figure 3D top row).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 3C and 3D

claim: Inflamed-III was characterized by a low frequency of CD45RA+ cells and high frequency of CD45RO+ and PD-1+ cells.
source: Inflamed-III was characterized by a low frequency of CD45RA+ cells and high frequency of CD45RO+ and PD-1+ cells (Figure 3C bottom, third row from top and Figure 3D middle row).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 3C and 3D

claim: Inflamed-IV was characterized by an enrichment of CD8+T cells expressing CD57, LAG-3, ICOS, Granzyme-B, PD-1 or CD45RO.
source: Inflamed-IV was characterized by an enrichment of CD8+T cells expressing CD57, LAG-3, ICOS, Granzyme-B, PD-1 or CD45RO (Figure 3C bottom, bottom row and Figure 3D bottom row).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 3C and 3D

claim: The phenotypes of CD8+T cells are coordinated across islets.
source: In summary, the phenotypes of CD8+T cells are coordinated across islets.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the identification of distinct inflamed sub-clusters

claim: Each donor possessed islets that belonged to multiple inflamed islet sub-clusters.
source: To identify cellular or molecular factors that regulate the state of CD8+T cells in islets, we first inspected the distribution of inflamed sub-clusters in each patient. Each donor possessed islets that belonged to multiple inflamed islet sub-clusters (Figure 3E).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3E

claim: Donor-level factors such as genetics, the location within the pancreas, or time since T1D onset are not associated with inflamed sub-clusters.
source: Therefore donor-level factors such as genetics, the location within the pancreas (i.e. head, body, or tail), or time since T1D onset, are not associated.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that each donor had multiple sub-clusters

claim: Insulitis sub-states are conserved among T1D patients.
source: Instead, these insulitis sub-states are conserved among T1D patients.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that sub-clusters are present across multiple donors

claim: For islets of Inflamed-II, -III, and -IV, functional markers characterizing their CD8+T cells were expressed more frequently inside than in the surrounding tissue areas.
source: We found that for islets of Inflamed-II, -III, and -IV, functional markers characterizing their CD8+T cells were expressed more frequently inside than in the surrounding tissue areas.
evidence: Direct statement of spatial analysis results

claim: The specific differences in the compositions of CD8+T cell states in different islets were attributable to the islet microenvironment and not the surrounding extra-islet spaces.
source: This demonstrated that the specific differences in the compositions of CD8+T cell states in different islets were attributable to the islet microenvironment and not the surrounding extra-islet spaces.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from spatial analysis showing enrichment of markers inside islets

claim: Neither the expression of markers of macrophage/DC activity nor macrophage/DC abundance was significantly associated with any of the inflamed sub-clusters.
source: Although macrophage/DCs are abundant in islets from the Inflamed group (Figure 2E, Figure 2F) and can interact with T cells by presenting antigen or secreting cytokines, neither the expression of markers of macrophage/DC activity nor macrophage/DC abundance was significantly associated with any of the inflamed sub-clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: No other cell type nor the vascular expression of IDO was linked to CD8+T cell programs in islets.
source: Similarly, no other cell type nor the vascular expression of IDO was linked to CD8+T cell programs in islets (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: The activation states of islet-infiltrating T cells are independent of the abundance of any of the other cell types identified.
source: Accordingly, the four inflamed sub-clusters had identical distributions throughout the original PAGA force-directed layout (Figure 3F). Therefore, the activation states of islet-infiltrating T cells are independent of the abundance of any of the other cell types we could identify.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that sub-clusters had identical distributions in pseudotime, shown in Figure 3F

claim: Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets contained a higher frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells and a lower frequency of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells than Inflamed islets.
source: Lastly, we compared CD8+T cells in islets from the Insulin-Depleted + Immune group to CD8+T cells in islets from the Inflamed group. Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets contained a higher frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells and a lower frequency of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells than Inflamed islets (Figure 3G).
evidence: Direct statement of comparison shown in Figure 3G

claim: TOX was expressed by a higher frequency of CD8+T cells in Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets than CD8+T cells in Inflamed islets.
source: TOX was expressed by a higher frequency of CD8+T cells in Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets than CD8+T cells in Inflamed islets (Figure 3G).
evidence: Direct statement of comparison shown in Figure 3G

claim: CD45RA and TOX were never co-expressed on the same CD8+T cell.
source: Importantly, CD45RA and TOX were never co-expressed on the same CD8+T cell (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The activation state or persistence of CD45RA+ and TOX+ CD8+T cell populations in islets depends on insulin expression.
source: These data indicate that the activation state or persistence of these two populations in islets depends on insulin expression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the differences in CD45RA+ and TOX+ T cells between Inflamed and Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets

claim: In the pancreas, islets are grouped within lobules.
source: In the pancreas, islets are grouped within lobules.
evidence: Statement of anatomical organization

claim: In some donors, the destruction of islets in T1D exhibits a strong lobular patterning.
source: In some donors, the destruction of islets in T1D exhibits a strong lobular patterning: that is, insulin-positive, immune-infiltrated, and insulin-negative islets are each primarily found in different lobules (Gepts, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gepts, 1965

claim: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) was used to quantify the degree of lobular patterning within each donor.
source: To systematically investigate lobular patterning in T1D, we used a neural network to segment lobules and assign each single cell and islet to its lobule. We first quantified the degree of lobular patterning within each donor using the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC).
evidence: Direct statement of methodology

claim: In the remaining cases (excluding non-T1D cases and cases 6314, 6195, and 6323), the ICCs ranged from 0.17 to 0.74.
source: Islets of non-T1D cases and 6314, 6195, and 6323 did not have appreciable variability in their pseudotimes, but in the remaining cases, the ICCs ranged from 0.17 to 0.74 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct statement of ICC values shown in Figure 4B

claim: The magnitude of lobular patterning ranges widely across T1D cases with insulitis.
source: This highlights that the magnitude of lobular patterning ranges widely across T1D cases with insulitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the range of ICC values

claim: Three cell types — vasculature, nerves, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells — were significantly associated with lobules across multiple T1D tissue donors.
source: We identified three cell types — vasculature, nerves, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells — that were significantly associated with lobules across multiple T1D tissue donors.
evidence: Direct statement of hierarchical linear modeling results

claim: Vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves were all more abundant in lobules with islets late in pseudotime.
source: All three were more abundant in lobules with islets late in pseudotime (Figure 4C boxed rows, Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 4C and 4D

claim: Samples from cases 6323 and 6195 had increased abundances of vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves in their extra-islet spaces compared to non-T1D controls.
source: Samples from cases 6323 and 6195 which had very few insulin-containing islets had increased abundances of vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves in their extra-islet spaces compared to non-T1D controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating these changes persist through the point when the entire tissue is afflicted.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves were increased in Inflamed islets compared to Normal islets.
source: In addition, vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves were increased in Inflamed islets compared to Normal islets indicating that they may serve a role in islets in addition to their role in the extra-islet compartment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Although CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs were higher in the extra-islet compartments of T1D cases vs non-T1D cases, they were not associated with lobular patterning.
source: Counterintuitively, although CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs were higher in the extra-islet compartments of T1D cases vs non-T1D cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), they were not associated with lobular patterning (they were not more abundant in the extra-islet space of lobules with more advanced insulitis; Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct statement with references to Figures 1—figure supplement 3 and 4C

claim: Vasculature, Granzyme-B/CD3- cells, and nerves outside islets may help predispose lobules to insulitis or are affected by extensive insulitis.
source: These data raise the possibility that vasculature, Granzyme-B/CD3- cells, and nerves outside islets help predispose lobules to insulitis or are affected by extensive insulitis.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the association between these cell types and lobular patterning

claim: Cellular neighborhoods (CNs) were identified by clustering single cells according to the cell type composition of their twenty nearest spatial neighbors.
source: Therefore, we identified cellular neighborhoods (CNs; Schürch et al., 2020; Bhate et al., 2022), tissue regions that are homogeneous and have defined cell type compositions. To identify CNs, single cells were clustered according to the cell type composition of their twenty nearest spatial neighbors and automatically annotated with the names of enriched cell types (Figure 5A, See Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement of methodology with reference to Figure 5A and citations

claim: 75 cellular neighborhoods (CNs) were identified.
source: This resulted in 75 CNs.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of CNs identified

claim: The top three CNs (by fold change of abundance in T1D relative to non-T1D) were (CD8+T cells|B cells), (Macrophage|Stromal Cells|B cells), and (Vasculature|B cells).
source: Next, we identified CNs that were more abundant in T1D than non-T1D tissues (Figure 5B). The top three CNs (fold change of abundance in T1D relative to abundance in non-T1D) were (CD8+T cells|B cells), (Macrophage|Stromal Cells|B cells), and (Vasculature|B cells) (Figure 5B, Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 5B and 5C

claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is predominantly found adjacent to both (Macrophage|Stroma|B cells) and (Vasculature|B cells) CNs.
source: Measuring the frequency with which the three B cell CNs were adjacent to each other throughout the tissues demonstrated that the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is predominantly found adjacent to both the other CNs but that (Macrophage|Stroma|B cells) and (Vasculature|B cells) are less commonly adjacent to each other (Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5D

claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN was not in the perivascular space.
source: Although the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN was adjacent to vessels (Figure 5D, Figure 5E), it was not in the perivascular space, as is the case with perivascular cuffs (Figure 5E).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figures 5D and 5E

claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN did not have segregated T cell and B cell zones as seen in mature TLSs.
source: In our samples, the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN did not have segregated T cell and B cell zones as seen in mature TLSs, consistent with previous reports (Korpos et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct observation with citation to Korpos et al., 2021

claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is more abundant in T1D tissues from patients with diabetes durations of 0–2 years compared to non-T1D tissues and T1D tissue from patients who had T1D for more than 4 years.
source: In summary, the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is more abundant in T1D tissues from patients with diabetes durations of 0–2 years compared to non-T1D tissues and T1D tissue from patients who had T1D for more than 4 years.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CN abundance analysis

claim: PNAd expression was observed in the vessels associated with the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN.
source: We observed expression of peripheral lymph node addressin (PNAd), an HEV marker, in the vessels associated with the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN (Figure 5E left image) but not in other vessels (data not shown).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Instances of the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN are immature TLSs.
source: Although we could not assess the presence of other TLS traits such as follicular dendritic cells, fibroblastic reticular cells, or follicular helper T cells, the aggregation of B cells and presence of HEVs, but the lack of compartmentalized B and T cell zones indicate that instances of the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN are immature TLSs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the presence of B cells, HEVs, and lack of segregated zones

claim: CD8+T cells co-expressing CD45RA and CD62L were observed near PNAd+ vasculature.
source: Next, we asked if immature TLSs could support the entry of naive CD8+T cells into the pancreas. We observed CD8+T cells co-expressing CD45RA and CD62L (the ligand for PNAd) near PNAd+ vasculature (Figure 5E, middle and right image respectively).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5E

claim: CD45RA+/CD8+T cells in the pancreas may adhere to HEVs.
source: Thus, CD45RA+/CD8+T cells in the pancreas may adhere to HEVs.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation of CD45RA+/CD62L+/CD8+T cells near PNAd+ vasculature

claim: CD45RA+ was enriched threefold on CD8+T cells in the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN relative to CD8+T cells in the tissue as a whole.
source: Furthermore, CD45RA+ was enriched threefold on CD8+T cells in the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN relative to CD8+T cells in the tissue as a whole (Figure 5F), providing additional evidence that CD45RA+ T cells may enter the pancreas through HEVs.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5F

claim: Immature TLSs were found both adjacent and not adjacent to islets.
source: We found immature TLSs both adjacent (Figure 5G.1) or not adjacent (Figure 5G.2) to islets.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Fewer than half of the immature TLSs were adjacent to islets.
source: Quantifying the frequency of this adjacency revealed that fewer than half of the immature TLSs were adjacent to islets (Figure 5H).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5H

claim: No differences were identified in the cellular composition of the immature TLSs that were or were not adjacent to islets.
source: We did not identify any differences in the cellular composition of the immature TLSs that were or were not adjacent to islets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Islet-adjacent CD45RA+/CD8+T cells co-expressed CD62L, suggesting that they originated from the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN.
source: We reasoned that even if immature TLSs were far from islets, extravasating cells may migrate to islets. Accordingly, islet-adjacent CD45RA+/CD8+T cells (that were not in islet-adjacent TLSs) co-expressed CD62L, suggesting that they originated from the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN (HH).
evidence: Inference drawn from the co-expression of CD45RA and CD62L on islet-adjacent T cells

claim: In one tissue donor, regions of the pancreas with Insulin-Depleted islets were enriched in the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN relative to regions with β-cell containing islets.
source: Consistent with this, in one notable tissue donor, regions of the pancreas with Insulin-Depleted islets were enriched in the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN relative to regions of the pancreas with β-cell containing islets (Figure 5J).
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5J

claim: The spatial correlation between the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN and the destruction of islets implicates immature TLSs with islet pathology even if they are not adjacent to islets.
source: This spatial correlation between the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN and the destruction of islets implicates immature TLSs with islet pathology even if they are not adjacent to islets (Figure 5J).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the spatial correlation shown in Figure 5J

claim: The results are consistent with the model previously proposed by Damond et al, who proposed a single trajectory for insulitis, characterized by an enrichment in HLA-ABC expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs.
source: First, our results are consistent with the model previously proposed by Damond et al, who proposed a single trajectory for insulitis, characterized by an enrichment in HLA-ABC expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs (Damond et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison of current results with previous model, supported by citation to Damond et al., 2019

claim: This is the first report that IDO+ vasculature is present in inflamed islets but not in normal islets or islets that have lost insulin-expression.
source: Second, we are the first to report that IDO+ vasculature is present in inflamed islets but not in normal islets or islets that have lost insulin-expression (Figure 2G, Figure 2H).
evidence: Direct statement of novel finding with references to Figures 2G and 2H

claim: Islets with IDO+ vasculature contained higher frequencies of CD8+T cells and higher expression of HLA-ABC, but not higher frequencies of macrophage/DCs compared to inflamed islets without IDO+ vasculature.
source: Furthermore, islets with IDO+ vasculature contained higher frequencies of CD8+T cells and higher expression of HLA-ABC, but not higher frequencies of macrophage/DCs compared to inflamed islets that did not contain IDO+ vasculature, suggesting that IDO is induced by a cytokine produced by infiltrating CD8+T cells such as IFN-γ (Figure 2I).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2I

claim: The loss of IDO on vasculature could be a prerequisite for β-cell death.
source: Given IDO's established tolerogenic role, these data suggest that the loss of IDO on vasculature could be a prerequisite for β-cell death.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the association between IDO+ vasculature and inflamed islets, and the known tolerogenic role of IDO

claim: Leveraging the IDO checkpoint to protect transplanted β-cells from rejection has shown promise.
source: Leveraging this checkpoint to protect transplanted β-cells from rejection has shown promise (Alexander et al., 2002) and could be combined with similar approaches using programmed death-ligand 1 (Yoshihara et al., 2020; Castro-Gutierrez et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alexander et al., 2002; Yoshihara et al., 2020; Castro-Gutierrez et al., 2021

claim: IDO expression on β-cells was not observed in this study, in contrast to Anquetil et al. who report this in healthy patients.
source: We did not observe IDO expression on β-cells, in contrast to Anquetil et al. that report this in healthy patients (Anquetil et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement of observation with citation to contrasting report

claim: The observations regarding IDO expression are consistent with data demonstrating that IDO needs to be induced.
source: Our observations are consistent with data demonstrating that IDO needs to be induced. First, it has been shown with western blot and RT-PCR that human islets require cytokine stimulation to express IDO (Sarkar et al., 2007). Second, the human protein atlas has tested multiple IDO antibodies and demonstrated that IDO is negative in human islets via immunohistochemistry: (https://www.proteinatlas.org). In addition, the human protein atlas's single-cell RNAseq atlas only report IDO transcripts in immune cells in healthy pancreas.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarkar et al., 2007 and reference to the Human Protein Atlas

claim: This study performed the first high-dimensional spatial phenotyping of CD8+T cells in T1D islets.
source: Third, we performed the first high-dimensional spatial phenotyping of CD8+T cells in T1D islets.
evidence: Direct statement of novel contribution

claim: Most T cells in islets were antigen experienced.
source: We found that most T cells were antigen experienced.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from marker expression analysis

claim: A small population of T cells expressed CD45RA and CD69, which could be naive, TEMRA, or Tscm cells.
source: A small population expressed CD45RA and CD69, which could be naive, TEMRA, or Tscm cells (P).
evidence: Observation with speculative interpretation based on marker expression

claim: Another population of T cells expressed LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS.
source: Another population expressed LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS.
evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis

claim: Only a small population of islets had Granzyme-B-expressing T cells.
source: It is notable that only a small population of islets had Granzyme-B-expressing T cells.
evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis

claim: The observation that only a small population of islets had Granzyme-B-expressing T cells could indicate that alternative mechanisms are contributing to the elimination of β-cells.
source: This could indicate that alternative mechanisms are contributing to the elimination of β-cells.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the observation of limited Granzyme-B expression

claim: The insulitis trajectory is comprised of four sub-clusters, each characterized by the activation profile of the islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells.
source: Fourth, the insulitis trajectory is comprised of four sub-clusters, each characterized by the activation profile of the islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3C

claim: Multiple inflamed sub-clusters were present in all T1D donors.
source: Multiple of these inflamed sub-clusters were present in all T1D donors (Figure 3E).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3E

claim: The T cell activation profiles characterizing each sub-cluster were only present in the islet, not in the surrounding tissue.
source: By phenotyping T cells at different distances from the islet edge, we were able to determine that the T cell activation profiles characterizing each sub-cluster were only present in the islet, not in the surrounding tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Pancreatic lobules affected by insulitis are characterized by distinct tissue markers.
source: Fifth, pancreatic lobules affected by insulitis are characterized by distinct tissue markers.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from hierarchical linear modeling analysis

claim: Lobules enriched in β-cell-depleted islets were also enriched in nerves, vasculature, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells.
source: We discovered that lobules enriched in β-cell-depleted islets were also enriched in nerves, vasculature, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, suggesting these factors may make lobules permissive to disease (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4C

claim: The Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells could be natural killer cells; if so, they are most likely of the CD56dim subset.
source: The Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells could be natural killer cells; if so, they are most likely of the CD56dim subset as CD56 was not detected on these cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on marker expression

claim: The cell types linked with direct islet invasion were distinct from those linked to lobule patterning.
source: It is noteworthy that the cell types linked with direct islet invasion were distinct from those linked to lobule patterning even though both sets of cell types were found across islet and extra-islet regions.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of cell types associated with different aspects of pathology

claim: For insulitis to consume every islet, crosstalk may be required between the cell types in the islet and extra-islet compartments.
source: Therefore, for insulitis to consume every islet, crosstalk may be required between the cell types in the islet and extra-islet compartments.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the observation of distinct cell types in different compartments

claim: Inhibiting the interaction between islet and extra-islet compartments might contain pathology to isolated lesions.
source: Conversely, inhibiting this interaction might contain pathology to isolated lesions.
evidence: Speculative therapeutic implication

claim: Immature TLSs were identified away from islets where CD45RA+/CD8+T cells aggregate.
source: Finally, we identify immature TLSs away from islets where CD45RA+/CD8+T cells aggregate.
evidence: Direct statement of finding

claim: An inflamed islet-subcluster characterized by an abundance of CD45RA+/CD8+ T cells was observed.
source: We also observed an inflamed islet-subcluster characterized by an abundance of CD45RA+/CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Direct statement of finding

claim: In mice, blocking immune egress from lymph nodes reduced the size of TLSs and halted diabetes.
source: In mice, blocking immune egress from lymph nodes reduced the size of TLSs and halted diabetes (Penaranda et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Penaranda et al., 2010

claim: Therapeutic targeting of immune cell trafficking to TLSs could help mitigate autoimmunity in human T1D.
source: Thus, therapeutic targeting of immune cell trafficking to TLSs could help mitigate autoimmunity in human T1D.
evidence: Speculative therapeutic implication based on mouse data

claim: These data illuminate relationships between insulitis, the local islet microenvironment and inflammation at distal sites.
source: Together, these data illuminate relationships between insulitis, the local islet microenvironment and inflammation at distal sites.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all findings

claim: A major limitation for the study is the cohort size.
source: A major limitation for the study is the cohort size.
evidence: Direct statement of study limitation

claim: Cases with documented insulitis are very rare, significantly limiting the feasibility of curating large cohorts.
source: Cases with documented insulitis are very rare, significantly limiting the feasibility of curating large cohorts (Campbell-Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: Explanation of limitation with supporting citation

claim: Factors such as the donors' histories of drug use, durations of stay in the intensive care unit, and BMIs could not be balanced or statistically adjusted for.
source: Due to this limitation, factors such as the donors' histories of drug use, durations of stay in the intensive care unit, and BMIs could not be balanced or statistically adjusted for but should be considered as they may affect exocrine inflammation but not the prevalence of insulitis (Bruggeman et al., 2021; In't Veld et al., 2010).
evidence: Direct statement of limitation with supporting citations

claim: Only one of the AA+ cases (Case 6267) had detectable insulitis.
source: In addition, only one of the AA+ cases, Case 6267, had detectable insulitis (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2C

claim: Case 6314 tested positive for only one autoantibody, GADA, and therefore had a significantly lower probability of progressing to overt T1D.
source: The other case, 6314 tested positive for only one autoantibody, GADA, and therefore had a significantly lower probability of progressing to overt T1D (Ziegler et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement with supporting citation to Ziegler et al., 2013

claim: The study failed to identify any heterogeneity in myeloid populations during insulitis.
source: Another limitation is our limited perspective on myeloid cell populations. Although antibodies in our panel detect numerous myeloid markers, we failed to identify any heterogeneity in myeloid populations during insulitis.
evidence: Direct statement of limitation

claim: The failure to identify myeloid heterogeneity was likely due in part to the difficulty of segmenting myeloid cells and quantifying marker expression due to their morphology.
source: This was likely due in part to the difficulty of segmenting myeloid cells and quantifying marker expression due to their morphology.
evidence: Explanation of limitation

claim: The samples are two-dimensional sections which could affect some of the adjacency relations.
source: Lastly, our samples are two-dimensional sections which could affect some of the adjacency relations.
evidence: Direct statement of limitation

claim: Using a data-driven approach, conserved sub-states of insulitis were mapped and the spatial pathology of islet and extra-islet regions was integrated into a single model of T1D pathogenesis.
source: In conclusion, using a data-driven approach, we mapped conserved sub-states of insulitis and integrated the spatial pathology of islet and extra-islet regions into a single model of T1D pathogenesis.
evidence: Summary statement of study contributions

claim: The tools and computational pipelines developed here will enable further investigation of immune pathology at the tissue scale that may lead to development of therapies for T1D.
source: The tools and computational pipelines developed here will enable further investigation of immune pathology at the tissue scale that may lead to development of therapies for T1D.
evidence: Statement of potential impact
